title: A barber who shaves everyone who doesn’t shave himself can’t exist
body: Picture a village barber who shaves all those, and only those, who do not shave themselves. Does he shave himself? If he does, he is someone the rule says he must not shave; if he doesn’t, the rule says he must. Every answer contradicts itself, so no such barber can exist. The puzzle is a homely version of Russell’s paradox about the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, though Russell, who had the barber suggested to him, called it an invalid form of his paradox.

slides.alt: Animation in a barbershop with turning striped poles: villagers sort themselves into ‘shaves himself’ and ‘shaved by the barber’. The barber tries each side, the rule crosses both out, and he fades to a dashed outline. Jars for sets then show the same flip-flop in Russell’s paradox.
slides.music: “Fig Leaf Rag” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: The barber shaves exactly those who don’t shave themselves. Put him on each side in turn; then try Russell’s set.
slides.takeaway: Both sides break the rule, so no such barber can exist, and nothing else is lost. Russell’s set fails the same way, but early set theory said it must exist, so its rules had to change.

slides.heading: Why every answer fails
slides.text: If the barber shaves himself, he is one of those who shave themselves, and the barber shaves none of them. If he doesn’t, he is one of those the barber must shave. No barber can follow the rule, so the question has no answer.

slides.heading: Does this collection include itself?

items.text: The set of everything that isn’t a square
A library catalogue that lists itself

slides.explanation: The set of squares isn’t a square, and the set of cats isn’t a cat. But the set of non-squares is itself not a square, so it is one of its own members.

left.label: The barber
left.text: No such barber can exist, so the question simply has no answer. Nothing else breaks.

right.label: Russell’s set
right.text: Early set theory let any property define a set, so the set of all sets that aren’t members of themselves had to exist. Its rules broke.

slides.heading: From a letter to new rules

events.text: He writes to Frege, whose logic it undermines
Type theory and Zermelo’s set theory avoid it
Russell calls the barber version not valid

slides.text: Hardly anything more unfortunate can befall a scientific writer than to have one of the foundations of his edifice shaken after the work is finished.
slides.attribution: Gottlob Frege, appendix to his Grundgesetze, vol. II (tr. Michael Beaney)

slides.heading: Not Russell’s barber
slides.text: The barber is often credited to Russell, for example by Martin Gardner. But Russell said it was suggested to him, and that in this form the contradiction is not very difficult to solve.

slides.question: Russell found his paradox in 1901. In 1902 he wrote about it to which logician, whose system it undermined?
slides.explanation: Frege was preparing the second volume of his Grundgesetze der Arithmetik. He replied quickly and added an appendix admitting the problem.
